name: Adenine
pairsWith: Thymine in DNA, Uracil in RNA
groupName: an amino group on the six-ring
groupWhat: A purine with –NH₂ at position 6. That NH₂ donates the hydrogen bonds it uses to pair.
note: Two rings fused. Pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds — the weaker of the two pairings, which is why AT-rich DNA melts first.

name: Guanine
groupName: a carbonyl and an amino group
groupWhat: A purine carrying =O at position 6 and –NH₂ at position 2. Two donors and an acceptor is what lets it make three hydrogen bonds.
note: The other purine. Pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, so GC-rich DNA takes more heat to separate.

name: Cytosine
groupName: a carbonyl and an amino group
groupWhat: A single ring with =O at position 2 and –NH₂ at position 4. The partner to guanine's three hydrogen bonds.
note: One ring. Present in both DNA and RNA, and the base that gets methylated to switch genes off.

name: Thymine
groupWhat: Uracil with a –CH₃ added at position 5. That methyl is the only difference between them, and it is how DNA is told apart from RNA.
note: DNA only. Thymine IS 5-methyluracil — remembering that one methyl is the whole distinction saves learning a fifth structure.

name: Uracil
groupWhat: A single ring with =O at positions 2 and 4, and nothing at 5. Thymine is this plus a methyl.
note: RNA only, standing in for thymine. Uracil is cheaper to make; DNA uses thymine so that deaminated cytosine, which becomes uracil, is recognisable as damage.
